rv.q: Or, more likely, Six Degrees transcends its particulars and addresses something ineffably human: The terrifying gulf between how we see ourselves and how we need others to see us.
The special beauty of this revival is that it is as comprehending of their shared plight as is the play.
It remains hugely entertaining, clever and provocative, especially in Cullman's superbly cast, high-octane production.
The writing is giddy with the excitement of ideas, some intentionally bogus, some inspirational.
The play still has a shimmering allure, thanks to its Albee-esque delight in language and its vivid portrayal of their willingness to be taken in by Paul’s reflected celebrity.
The cumulative effect, once you get over the retro vibe, is renewed respect for a disquieting, still-rewarding work.

Mr. Hawkins, best known for his performance as Dr. Dre in the film “Straight Outta Compton,” gives us a Paul who is a truth-teller in spite of himself.
Despite the vitalizing presence of Allison Janney in director Trip Cullman's elegant revival, "Six Degrees of Separation" lacks the comic bite of the original production.
And so Ouisa’s journey of self-revelation — her discovery of a profound, potentially life-changing compassion for and intimacy with Paul — rings hollow in a way it did not before.

Trip Cullman’s dazzling production captures the play’s many qualities as a dizzying farce, a gossipy one-on-one conversation, an attention-grabbing lecture, a drama about personal connection and a disturbing portrait of economic inequality and racial division.
His is a performance of size and scope that is, in a word, dazzling.

“Six Degrees of Separation” – yes, long before Kevin Bacon, this is where the phrase originated – is a rollicking ninety minutes and not for the tame of heart.

She’s one of that rare ones who can make you laugh as hard as she can make you cry.
Six Degrees of Separation, as seen here, is a great play with great performances but very much a creature of its time.
My biggest complaint about the play is the episode in which “Paul” cons two young would-be actors from Utah (Peter Mark Kendall and Sarah Mezzanotte) with tragic results.
It's a feat for a charming, magnetic conman (such as the real one who partly inspired Guare's 1990 play), but here the conceit is less than wholly convincing.
The show does expose readiness and willingness to be hustled.
Happily, Guare’s script is unscathed by the vagaries of time: it’s as wonderful—and as fresh—as ever.
It is now having its first Broadway revival, and it’s as sharp and delightful as ever, skewering white liberal guilt, societal racism, and the child-rearing of the wealthy with glee and wit to spare.
Everything’s done just a little bit bigger than it needs to be.
Although the show has many funny lines, ultimately Six Degrees should be presented as a tragedy, and Mr. Cullman just misses the mark in all the wrong places.

cn.t: Critics praise this stylish revival for Janney's commanding performance and Guare's sharp writing, though many find Cullman's direction too broad and farcical, undermining the play's deeper emotional resonance and tonal shifts.

sg.ra: TickPick and Headout both name Center Orchestra rows E-J (TickPick: E-J; SeatPlan/Headout: F-O) as the prime zone at the Barrymore because the 1,058-seat house is shallow enough that the mezzanine overhang only kicks in at row K of the orchestra, leaving center rows F-J with an uncovered, forward sightline well-suited to the text-driven plays this house tends to book.

Headout and TickPick both warn against Orchestra rows A-C at the Barrymore specifically because the stage at this 1928 house sits high relative to the front rows — TickPick: 'rows A, B, and C are too close to the stage and might block your view'; Headout adds that 'seats closer to the stage may cause neck strain from looking upward.'

SeatPlan and TickPick both confirm the Barrymore mezzanine overhang begins at row K of the orchestra but isn't obstructive — SeatPlan: 'those sitting in the rear of the Orchestra section will notice that the stage feels impressively close'; the house's well-raked orchestra keeps sightlines intact even under cover, which matters because this is a 1,058-seat intimate-play house and losing the rear orchestra would shrink the good-seat pool significantly.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, under premium pricing
sg.ra: SeatPlan directly names row A Center Front Mezzanine as the house favorite at the Barrymore — 'very popular thanks to its fantastic elevated position above the stage' — and both SeatPlan and TickPick emphasize the Barrymore's front mezzanine is only 5 rows deep (A-E, 196 seats), so even row E retains a wide, pitched view and benefits from the intimate 1,058-seat scale.

SeatPlan specifically praises the Barrymore rear mezzanine rake: 'a decent rake means even the back rows offer a surprisingly good look at the stage' and 'even in the far corner theatergoers won't feel too much strain to make out the stage.' The house's three-flights-up rear mezz is the trade-off for the small footprint, but the rake compensates for distance in a way deeper houses don't manage.

Headout and TickPick both flag the Barrymore's six box seats (three per side of the orchestra) and the orchestra rows D-E directly beneath them as compromised — Headout: 'seats under the Boxes in rows D and E a little restricted'; TickPick adds 'far Left and Right Orchestra and the outer corners of the Mezzanine can have reduced sightlines.' This is a specific quirk of the Barrymore's 1928 proscenium layout with built-in side boxes.
